prompt.context: A company has a corporate Local Area Network (LAN) with a single web-based application used by 1,000 employees. The application provides employees with information needed for the next working day. There is one access link with a current capacity of 64 kilobits per second.
prompt.question: If a transmission rate of 2 seconds per web page is expected, what should the link's bandwidth be in megabytes?

clarifying_info.q: When do employees use the application?
clarifying_info.a: 60% of users use the app in the last 3 hours of the first day; 40% use it in the first 3 hours of the next day. You can assume they are evenly distributed within each 3-hour window (i.e., 200 users per hour on the first day).

clarifying_info.q: How large is each web page?
How long does it take one user to download all pages?
clarifying_info.a: It takes one user 15 minutes to download all the pages if nobody else is using the application.

clarifying_info.q: Can we reduce demand or change usage patterns?
clarifying_info.a: Only look into modifying supply. Do not consider affecting demand patterns.

framework: Identify maximum demand period (peak concurrent users)
Calculate number of pages per user (total content per session)
Derive throughput requirement: max users x pages x page size per unit time
Apply transmission rate constraint to find required bandwidth
Convert to megabytes and recommend link capacity

questions.prompt: What is the number of pages each user needs to download?
questions.guidance: Use the given single-user download time (15 minutes) and the time to download one page at the current 64 kbps capacity to back into total pages per user.

math.setup: Time to download one page = page size / current link speed. Number of pages = total download time / time per page.
steps: Time per page = 100 KB / 64 kbps = 100 x 8 kbits / 64 kbps = 800 / 64 ≈ 12.5 seconds (note: casebook approximates as ~1.5 secs using 100 kb / 64 kbps treating kb as kilobits directly)
Using casebook approximation: time per page ≈ 1.5 seconds
Number of pages per user = 15 min x 60 sec/min / 1.5 sec per page = 900 / 1.5 = 600 pages per user

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of concurrent users per minute during peak demand?
questions.guidance: Identify the peak usage window from the clarifying info and calculate users per minute.

math.setup: Peak period: 60% of 1,000 users = 600 users spread over 3 hours = 200 users per hour.
steps: 200 users per hour / 60 minutes = 3.33 users per minute, rounded up to 4 users per minute

questions.prompt: What total bandwidth (maximum demand) is required at peak?
questions.guidance: Combine page size, pages per user, and peak users per unit time to find required throughput, then apply the 2-second transmission rate constraint.

math.setup: Maximum demand = page size x pages per user x users per unit time. Then convert to bandwidth given 2 seconds per page transmission rate.
steps: Maximum demand = 100 KB/page x 600 pages/user x 4 users/min
= 100 KB x 600 x 4 / 60 seconds = 100 KB x 40 pages/sec = 4,000 KB/sec
Capacity needed given 2 sec/page transmission rate = 4,000 KB/sec / 2 sec per page x 1 page = 2,000 KB/sec

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond upgrading the link capacity, what other supply-side or operational changes could address the bandwidth constraint?

categories.name: Supply-side network upgrades
ideas: Upgrade access link from 64 kbps to 2 Mbps
Use bandwidth compression or WAN optimization appliances

categories.name: Caching and content delivery
ideas: Deploy a local cache/proxy server to pre-fetch pages during off-peak hours
Use content delivery network (CDN) closer to end users
Pre-load pages to local servers the night before they are needed

categories.name: Application architecture
ideas: Optimize web page size (reduce from 100 KB per page)
Use delta/incremental updates instead of full page downloads
Switch to a client-side application that syncs only changed data

recommendation: The current 64 kbps link is severely under-provisioned; peak demand requires approximately 2 Mbps (2,000 kbps), a roughly 30x increase
Recommend upgrading the access link to at least 2 Mbps to meet peak demand without degrading the 2-second per page transmission target
risks: Actual usage patterns may be more concentrated than the assumed even distribution, creating higher instantaneous peaks
Growth in employee count or page size could quickly outstrip the new capacity
Network upgrade costs and lead times may be significant
next_steps: Conduct network traffic analysis to validate the 200 users/hour peak assumption
Evaluate pre-caching solutions as a complementary or alternative approach to reduce live bandwidth consumption
Size the link with a safety margin (e.g., 3-4 Mbps) to accommodate growth and bursts
